must_allow.text: HbA1c measures the average share of hemoglobin that has glucose attached over roughly the past three months.
LDL cholesterol is reported in mg/dL in the United States and in mmol/L in many other countries.
Fasting means not eating or drinking anything except water for a set number of hours before the blood draw.
A reference range is the span of values seen in most healthy people tested by a given lab.
Creatinine is a waste product from muscle that the kidneys filter out of the blood.
A complete blood count reports red cells, white cells, and platelets.
eGFR is an estimate of kidney filtering that is calculated from creatinine, age, and sex.
TSH is made by the pituitary gland and signals the thyroid to release hormones.
Blood is usually drawn from a vein in the arm using a small needle.
Ferritin reflects the amount of iron stored in the body.
Triglycerides are a type of fat carried in the blood, and levels rise after a meal.
ALT is an enzyme found mostly in liver cells.
Reference ranges can differ between labs because of different equipment and populations.
Hemoglobin carries oxygen in red blood cells.
A urinalysis checks a urine sample for things such as protein, glucose, and blood cells.
Units matter: 5.5 mmol/L of glucose is about 99 mg/dL.
Some tests are done fasting because eating can temporarily raise glucose and triglycerides.
Potassium is an electrolyte that helps nerves and muscles work.
Vitamin B12 is needed to make red blood cells and to keep nerves healthy.
A lipid panel usually includes total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides.
INR is a measure of how long blood takes to clot.
Results flagged H or L simply mean the value is above or below the lab's reference range.
Platelets are small cell fragments that help blood clot.
The sodium level in blood reflects the balance of salt and water in the body.
The mean corpuscular volume describes the average size of red blood cells.
High LDL cholesterol can be seen in people with inherited lipid disorders, diets high in saturated fat, or an underactive thyroid.
A low hemoglobin may be associated with iron deficiency, vitamin deficiencies, or chronic disease.
Raised creatinine is one of several possible signs of reduced kidney function.
Elevated ALT can occur with fatty liver, viral hepatitis, certain medicines, and other causes.
A high TSH is often seen in people whose thyroid is underactive.
Low ferritin is commonly seen in people with iron deficiency.
High fasting glucose is sometimes seen in people with diabetes, but also with stress or illness.
Low vitamin B12 may be associated with certain digestive conditions and some diets.
Elevated white blood cell counts can happen with infection, inflammation, or some medicines.
Low sodium has many possible causes, including some medicines and fluid imbalance.
High potassium may be linked to kidney problems or to certain blood pressure medicines, among other reasons.
Dehydration is one of several possible reasons for a temporarily raised creatinine.
High triglycerides are sometimes associated with excess alcohol or sugar intake and with some conditions.
Low platelet counts may be seen in people with a range of conditions, from viral infections to bone marrow disorders.
Protein in the urine can be associated with kidney disease, but also with fever or heavy exercise.
High uric acid levels are found in many people with gout, though many people with high levels never develop it.
A low white cell count can sometimes be seen after a viral illness or with certain drugs.
Elevated HbA1c is associated with higher average blood glucose over recent months.
High ferritin can be linked to inflammation, liver conditions, or iron overload.
Low vitamin D is common in people who get little sun exposure.
Raised CRP is a general marker that may be associated with infection or inflammation.
Low TSH may be seen in people with an overactive thyroid, among other reasons.
Some people with mildly raised liver enzymes have no underlying disease at all.
A high red cell count can occur at high altitude, in smokers, or with some blood disorders.
A slightly high calcium level may sometimes be associated with parathyroid gland activity.
